extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a proposed invention meets the legal qualities (novelty, sufficiency of invention, utility, claim scope) required for a patent, illustrated by case examples and judicial tests. Focuses on how courts assess change, result, combination of elements, and claim breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of invention — change and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of invention sufficient to support a patent is estimated from a compound view of the change effected and the consequences of that change; view the change and its consequences as a sum to decide if both taken together are considerable or unimportant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very slight or accidental change may be sufficient if it leads to consequences of great practical utility (examples: Dudley's, Crane's, Hall's, Daniel's inventions). If both the change and its consequences are inconsiderable, sufficiency of invention is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requisites: novelty and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statute the question of patentability depends on satisfying the requisites of novelty and utility, after the subject is ascertained to belong to a statutory class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply tests and illustrations drawn from decisions to determine the proper scope and application of novelty and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty defined by substantial difference; focus on result
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter is new when it is substantially different from what has gone before; courts examine the character of the result, not the apparent amount of skill or ingenuity exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the result is substantially different from prior art, the invention is likely entitled to a patent; otherwise it fails. (See Kneass v. Schuylkill Bank example and related discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Change must produce a different effect or principle (not merely form/proportion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere change of form or proportion is not necessarily a discovery; if changing form/proportion produces a new effect, it embodies a change of principle and may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Justice Marshall's test: the word 'simply' is important — only changes that are 'simply' form/proportion and nothing more are excluded. If the change yields a beneficial different result to a considerable degree, that supports patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement must be beneficial to the trade / public (improvement_of_trade test)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention should be an 'improvement of the trade' — i.e., beneficial to the manufacture/trade of the article — to be substantive; mere changes that affect only the mode of selling without improving the article itself are frivolous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: labeling/wrapping imported cotton so it sells at a higher price without altering the article was held frivolous and not patentable. Ornamental objects that are bought for decoration differ because the ornament is intrinsic to use; mere sales-packaging that is stripped before use is not an improvement of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent limited to the actual invention; cannot claim whole machine for a mere improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patentee adds a mere improvement to an existing machine, a patent cannot be for the whole machine but only for the improvement; the scope of the patent is limited to the patentee's actual invention or new combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If separate stages/effects were previously produced by separate machines or known combinations, simply combining them does not sustain a patent for the entire combined machine (Whittemore v. Cutter, watch/steam-engine analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot patent an effect only; must claim a mode or peculiar manner of producing it
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent can be obtained for an effect alone (e.g., admeasurement of time, expansive operations of steam); patents are for a new mode or new application of machinery to produce an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim framed as for an effect without specifying the mode/operation will be invalid; courts look for the modus operandi or peculiar device described in the specification/claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution or application of known means to similar uses often not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a well-known mode or well-practised means to a circumstance extremely similar to prior art often amounts to mere mechanical skill and is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: making anchor flukes integral with a conical hole to avoid welding was held to be the simple application of a known mode; substitution of a broad-headed stay in a link might support a patent only if, in connection with governing principles and utility, it is shown to be new and beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of known ingredients may be patentable if the combination is new
rubrics_metrics.description: If materials/ingredients have been used before, the true question is whether the particular combination used by the patentee is substantially new; a new combination that produces a new useful result is patentable even if individual ingredients are old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friction-match example: none of the ingredients needed be new, but if they were never combined in that manner to produce the result claimed, the combination is patentable. Simplicity of combination is not an objection and may be a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of an old contrivance to a new purpose may be insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere application of an old contrivance to a new purpose (i.e., using known apparatus in a new context) is insufficient if the same apparatus or machinery had long been in use for similar purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reclining and fixing a chair-back by apparatus long used in other machines was void because it accomplished nothing not done before; courts distinguish where a new combination of apparatus was not previously known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test whether the same effects are produced by the same mode (principles vs effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same effects are produced by the same mode of operation, the principles are the same; if the same effects are produced by a substantially different combination or mode, the principles differ and may be new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multi-stage machines, identify the separate stages/effects and compare whether those effects were produced before by substantially the same machinery/mode; jury fact-finding often required (Whittemore machine stages example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of achievement is not fatal; simple inventions can be highly valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent simplicity of an invention does not disqualify it; producing a great result by very simple means can be the highest class of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts explicitly reject 'simplicity' as a negative criterion (see Story's discussion in the friction-match case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior analogous structures may defeat novelty unless differences are radical
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art shows striking analogies, a patent may still be valid if the differences between the prior structure and the claimed invention are not merely mechanical but radical in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may rely on scientific expert testimony to determine whether differences are 'radical' (Blandy v. Griffith bed-plate: continuous shell + lateral attachment vs earlier frames).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antedating prior art that differs only in surface detail may render claim unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: If prior art is substantially the same in combination and arrangement and the claimed change is merely a surface modification (e.g., engraving a previously smooth roller), the invention may be considered mere mechanical skill and not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stimpson v. Woodman: figured roller versus smooth roller; substitution of an old figured roller for the purpose was held not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be construed to the essence of the invention as described
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts construe patent claims to embrace the specific elements described in the specification; the essence of the invention is determined by construction of the claim and the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the portable steam-engine case the court construed the claim to three elements (hollow continuous bed-plate between boiler and engine; cast flanges on upper and outer side; attachment of operative parts to those flanges) and held the essence to be the bed-plate construction and lateral attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to mere articles of known material shaped or with obvious additions are invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that effectively covers a known material (e.g., 'an elastic eraser pencil head' viewed as 'a piece of india-rubber with a hole') is invalid for want of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will treat attempts to monopolize a known substance with trivial modifications as insufficient; the claim must reflect a new mode, combination or principle.
